For FD002, normalized XGBoost reduced terminal RMSE yet increased the asymmetric NASA score (12,616 to 13,289). Additional model-seed, condition count, RUL-cap, grouped-validation and explanation checks test sensitivity rather than postulating a universally optimal representation. The six clusters reproduce known simulator operating regimes; no new condition discovery algorithm, causal diagnostic method, or field ready prognostic system is claimed. Since the official test endpoints were also used in earlier exploratory comparisons, all newly examined alternatives are reported as retrospective benchmark evidence, not as results from a pristine confirmatory holdout.

entries.title: The Complexity of Oracle-Efficient Realizable Transductive Learning
entries.abstract: In realizable transductive online learning, the learner knows the entire sequence of T instances in advance, and the labels are consistent with one of N hypotheses. With explicit access to the hypothesis class, the halving algorithm makes at most log₂ N mistakes. Can a comparable guarantee be achieved using only polynomially many empirical risk minimization (ERM) queries? We answer this question negatively, even for a weighted-ERM oracle that optimizes arbitrary real-valued linear objectives and returns a complete maximizing hypothesis. For every fixed β∈(0,1) and every randomized learner making polynomially many oracle queries, there exists a fixed realizable instance with exactly N=2^(⌊T^β⌋) hypotheses on which the learner makes Ω_β(√TlogN) mistakes in expectation. This matches the agnostic-rate upper bound achieved by random playout using O(T) oracle calls. The separation persists for much smaller classes as well: along a sequence with logN=Θ((logT)²), we establish a mistake lower bound of exp(Ω(logT/loglogT)). Our main technical contribution is a composition lemma that combines two realizable prediction problems such that their mistake lower bounds add, up to a small loss, while keeping the growth of the combined hypothesis class under control. Iterating this lemma yields a family of hard instances spanning the desired parameter regimes, establishing a sharp separation between information-theoretic and oracle-efficient mistake guarantees.
entries.comment: 22 pages, 1 figure; fixed LaTeX \Cref issues in v1. No changes to the content

entries.title: UNIFY: Unified Learning with One Model via Batch Norm Switching
entries.abstract: Neural networks are typically trained separately for individual datasets or tasks, resulting in many task-specific models. This redundancy increases memory footprint, deployment costs, and energy consumption limiting their scalability. We propose UNIFY, a unified learning framework that enables a single model to jointly learn and perform inference across multiple datasets via Batch Normalization Switching (BNS). Instead of maintaining separate models for each dataset, UNIFY shares the parameter-intensive backbone while maintaining dataset-specific BN statistics and parameters, along with dataset-specific classification heads. We validate our framework using five datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet) across six Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) of different sizes (SqueezeNet 1.1, WideResNet-40-2, WideResNet-16-8, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50). Notably, a single UNIFIED ResNet-34 trained on these datasets achieves accuracies of 99.53%, 94.84%, 96.12%, 80.32%, and 67.67%, respectively, outperforming the average performance of the corresponding independently trained task-specific models while reducing the memory footprint by approximately 4.94x, from 428.30 MB (five separate models) to 86.71 MB (one unified model). UNIFY aims not only to consolidate (K) models into a single model but also to enhance model-effectiveness by leveraging complementary knowledge across datasets. It paves the way for scalable, efficient, and unified learning capable of handling diverse image classification tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/saktx/UNIFY.

entries.title: How many mistakes does it take to learn an interval? Exact Littlestone dimensions of intervals and their unions
entries.abstract: The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of j intervals on m points, only its order of growth was known. We determine it exactly. For every switch budget k (with both end labels fixed when k is odd), the smallest size on which d mistakes can be forced follows a three-regime law: d+1 while d≤k, then 2d-k+1, and beyond d=⌈3k/2⌉+k-1 doubling the size adds exactly k mistakes. Unions of j intervals on m points correspond to k=2j and size m+1, and a single interval gives the thresholds 1,2,3,5,7,10,14,20,…. The natural learner that waits for a positive example and binary-searches both endpoints is not optimal: it can be forced into one extra mistake for 50,847 of the domain sizes below 10⁵. Upper bounds come from a gap potential and a block-pairing learner, and lower bounds from adversary strategies and a refinement step. These tools give an explicit optimal learner with O(logm) time per round, which on random streams makes more mistakes on average than the natural learner. For randomised learners, we compute the randomised Littlestone dimension of thresholds exactly and prove that a greedy adversary forces an explicit closed-form number of expected mistakes on intervals; this bound is within 0.64 of optimal and, we conjecture, exact (confirmed for m≤70). Exact computation tests every result, and the formulas for every switch budget are machine-checked in Lean 4.
entries.comment: 33 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables. Code and Lean 4 proofs: https://github.com/researchbackup27-sudo/exact-littlestone-intervals

entries.title: Routing Collapse in Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts: Cross-Modal Conditioning Restores Expert Diversity Without Improving Accuracy
entries.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifiers are increasingly applied to multimodal emotion recognition, yet the health of their routing distributions is rarely measured. We study a seven-expert MoE head on IEMOCAP under two conditions that differ only in how modality embeddings are fused before reaching it: a learned scalar gate alone, and the same gate preceded by pairwise cross-modal attention. Under scalar fusion the router collapses, concentrating on 1.88 of seven experts at a normalised entropy of 0.241. Cross-modal fusion raises entropy to 0.537 and utilisation to 3.25 experts, a 2.23x increase (p=0.035, Cohen's d=2.55), and induces emotion-differentiated routing absent in the scalar case. This recovered diversity confers no detectable benefit: across six seeds per condition, weighted accuracy (p=0.646) and run-to-run variance (p=0.768) are statistically indistinguishable. We further observe a 13-point accuracy spread under identical configuration. In this regime, router health and task performance are decoupled, and diagnosing collapse does not by itself justify fixing it.

entries.title: CLAIR: Consistent LLM Adaptation via Index-free Reprogramming
entries.abstract: Time-series forecasting with pretrained large language models (LLMs) uses contextualized patch representations, raising the question of how to align them. Matching patches at the same temporal position is natural, but self-attention allows each patch state to incorporate information from elsewhere in the input window, suggesting that useful correspondences can extend across positions. This flexibility, however, does not necessarily translate into consistent forecasts: similar patch states may play different roles when used in their original temporal order. To address both issues, we propose CLAIR (Consistent LLM Adaptation via Index-free Reprogramming), a teacher-guided framework that combines patch-level transport alignment (PTA) and forecast-level consistency (FC). A clean-view exponential moving average (EMA) teacher guides a mildly perturbed student, with PTA establishing soft, representation-dependent correspondences and FC encouraging agreement at corresponding future steps. The forecasting head retains the original patch order. We test this combination through controlled comparisons: while PTA and index-wise alignment perform similarly without FC, PTA+FC under EMA supervision reduces horizon-averaged mean squared error (MSE) by 2.1% on ETTh1 and 2.6% on ETTm1 relative to Index+FC. The same preference for PTA+FC emerges in comparisons with alternative matching strategies on Weather and ETTh2. Beyond these controls, CLAIR achieves the lowest horizon-averaged MSE on five of six long-term benchmarks and the lowest aggregate overall weighted average (OWA) on M4 among evaluated methods, with competitive few-shot performance. As the teacher and transport are used only during training, inference requires only the student.

entries.title: Training speech deepfake detectors against worst-case filters: Gains, Costs and Limits
entries.abstract: Speech deepfake detectors make few errors on standard benchmarks, yet a simple attack defeats them: the attacker passes fake speech through one short filter, tuned against the detector, and many fakes then pass as real. Training with random filters does not stop this attack, because the attacker uses the worst filter, not a random one. We therefore train the detector against the worst case: during training, a small set of filters is updated to fool the current detector, at about the cost of random filters. In a preregistered study, this made the detector more robust to filter attacks on real-world recordings than random filters did. It also lowered the in-domain attack error of the standard detector, and beat one-step adversarial training with additive noise on real-world recordings. The price is a higher error on unfiltered speech, and a validation study shows that choosing the checkpoint on held-out spoofing systems made the standard detector about as robust.

entries.title: Peel, Don't Whack: Partial Coverage, Imperfect Validators, and Intervention Based Shortcut Mitigation
entries.abstract: Without group labels, shortcut mitigation increasingly relies on interventions: label-preserving edits, such as background or watermark replacement, that are proposed automatically and accepted by a validator. Invariance to a complete family of valid edits yields robustness, but in practice coverage is partial and validators err. We analyze both in a stylized linear model. For the population logistic solution and the max-margin limit of gradient descent, the decision on every shortcut-flip group follows one additive rule. Hence worst-group accuracy never decreases with coverage, while individual groups can provably degrade, a mechanism for the Whac-a-Mole effect; full coverage is not always needed. In the logistic regime the validator's false-accept rate must stay below a closed-form tolerance that grows with coverage. With noiseless training data, one false accept can make the max-margin solution ignore the core. In this model, sensitivity-based discovery removes shortcuts in decreasing salience. We also give a model-agnostic certificate, valid under content-independent validation, whose validator-error term comes from an audit. Simulations match the theory, and deep networks on synthetic and real images show the predicted Whac-a-Mole signs, monotone worst-group accuracy and validator fragility. The resulting procedure, Peel (Propose-Edit-Evaluate-Learn), can propose candidate edits from the model's own mistakes. Given an oracle library of the benchmarks' intervention operators, it selects the right ones and beats group-label methods on Waterbirds and UrbanCars. With fully generated edits, run end to end from three discovery seeds, it improves on empirical risk minimization (ERM) on five of six benchmarks but trails exact edits.

entries.title: Wavelet-CFM for the extragalactic millimeter-wave sky
entries.abstract: We develop a Wavelet-factorized Conditional Flow Matching (Wavelet-CFM) framework to generate fast, accurate simulations of correlated astrophysical fields including gravitational lensing convergence (κ), the kinetic and thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ and tSZ) effects, and cosmic infrared background (CIB) emission. Together these make up every bright extragalactic component of the millimeter-wave (mm-wave) sky apart from radio sources. Our approach combines multi-scale wavelet decomposition with conditional flow matching models, trained on ~9×9 deg² patches at 1-arcminute resolution. The four fields are generated jointly, including their cross couplings, and the model has a tractable likelihood, which to our knowledge has not previously been achieved for this set of components. The power spectra, one-point distributions and Minkowski functionals of the generated maps match a validation set to a few percent. These results show promise for enabling field-level cosmological analyses of mm-wave data.
entries.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Accepted to the 9th Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences Workshop (ML4PS)

entries.title: DeCo: Decoupled Traffic State Modeling with Cross-Variable Coordination
entries.abstract: Accurate forecasts of traffic flow, occupancy, and speed are essential for congestion management and travel planning. These variables exhibit distinct spatiotemporal patterns, and their coupled dynamics characterize the evolution of traffic conditions, such as the onset and dissipation of congestion. Existing methods often either neglect this coupling or struggle to capture the distinct dynamics of all three variables within a unified model. In this paper, we propose DeCo, a decoupled traffic state modeling framework with cross-variable coordination for forecasting flow, occupancy, and speed. Specifically, DeCo first trains a dedicated forecaster for each variable to specialize in its unique spatiotemporal dynamics. It then estimates a residual correction for each forecast by jointly leveraging the predicted trajectories and recent observations of all three variables, thereby exploiting cross-variable coupling and mitigating systematic prediction errors. We extend the flow-only PeMS03 and PeMS07 benchmarks to all three variables on their original sensors and release the aligned data. Experiments on PeMS03, PeMS04, PeMS07, and PeMS08 show that DeCo achieves the lowest mean absolute error for every variable on every dataset, up to 4.9% below RAGC, the strongest baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/lixus7/DeCo.

entries.title: The Evaluation Substrate Matters: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Serving Substrates
entries.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) usually coordinate heterogeneous models and tools to solve complex tasks, creating a growing need for reliable evaluation. However, a multi-agent workflow that is fastest in one serving environment can lose its advantage in another, even when its models, prompts, and task remain fixed. This makes a benchmark result conditional on how the workflow is executed. We introduce MASSys, a benchmark for measuring this dependence in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. MASSys executes the same candidate-task pairs across serving substrates and load regimes, using five workload families spanning software repair, research synthesis, financial analysis, interactive control, and diagram generation. It records task quality alongside delivery, latency, cost, resource pressure, and failure evidence. In a controlled motivation diagnostic, the Star workflow falls from first to fourth in mean-latency rank under KV-cache pressure, while Chain rises from fourth to first. The substrate sweeps further show that increasing load creates long runtime tails and timeout pressure. In several task families, quality among evaluated outputs changes less than effective quality over submitted jobs: the system delivers fewer usable results even when the surviving outputs remain competitive. Tool and runtime traces reveal that these outcomes involve both model serving and non-model execution. Together, the results motivate evaluating MAS designs over explicit operating conditions and reporting which tasks are delivered, how well they are solved, and where execution breaks down.
entries.comment: Code: https://github.com/MAS-Sys-Bench/MAS-Sys ; Project page: https://mas-sys-bench.github.io/MAS-Sys-Page/ ; Trace dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/MAS-Sys/MAS-Sys-Traces

entries.title: Physical regime changes expose formula misuse in large language models
entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for scientific computing across the Earth and environmental sciences, but problems in these fields often involve distinct physical regimes. LLMs may fail to recognize these regime-dependent constraints, applying formulas outside their domains of validity and producing plausible but physically incorrect results. We systematically investigate these failures through controlled experiments and assess whether post-training can improve regime-aware reasoning. Across 72 physical mechanisms, we find frontier LLMs frequently misapply formulas outside their regimes of validity, reducing accuracy by 13-57 percentage points. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards enables Qwen3.5-9B to match DeepSeek V4 Flash (284B) on regime-dependent tasks, but its effectiveness is limited by the formulas available in the base model. Combining supervised fine-tuning on a few worked examples with reinforcement learning improves accuracy by 61 percentage points, while distillation from a teacher supplied with the correct formula raises accuracy from 0% to 71%.
entries.comment: 19 pages, 9 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Information appended. Code and data: https://github.com/acodercat/AtmosRegime

entries.title: UACR: Uncertainty-Aware Collaborative Routing for Explainable Industrial Anomaly Inspection
entries.abstract: Industrial anomaly inspection requires not only accurate anomaly discrimination but also trustworthy explanations for operators, while satisfying the strict latency constraints of online inspection. Existing methods, however, typically apply a fixed computational path to all samples, making it difficult to strike a good balance among detection accuracy, inference efficiency, and interpretability. To address this issue, we propose UACR, an uncertainty-aware collaborative routing framework for explainable industrial anomaly inspection. UACR aims to deliver reliable anomaly decisions together with operator-facing explanations under the online inspection budget, while adaptively allocating computation so that ambiguous cases receive deeper scrutiny. The framework consists of two stages. Stage I, Offline Training and Routing Hyperparameter Search, learns the anomaly inspection modules and calibrates the uncertainty estimator that drives routing. Stage II, Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Routing, collaboratively dispatches each input across inspection paths according to its estimated uncertainty. Experimental results on multiple public datasets show that UACR achieves over 5.16% improvement in accuracy compared to the baseline method, while reducing latency by over 31.5%. It also enhances the interpretability of industrial detection by over 15%.

entries.title: Stein Guidance without Gradients: Discretization Uniform Diffusion Inference Time Scaling beyond Particle SMC
entries.abstract: Reward-guided diffusion requires effective steering and correction of the bias introduced by approximate value functions. A Brownian example shows that SMC with full multinomial resampling at every step can require particle counts to grow linearly with guidance depth to maintain accuracy. We propose Stein Guidance, which combines derivative-free guidance with whole-path independence Metropolis-Hastings correction. Value-weighted selection from centered Gaussian candidates approximates gradient guidance in expectation, using as few as two queries per step. Centering stabilizes the local normalizer estimates, and the same queries yield an explicit path weight for correction. Under uniform value and spatial regularity bounds, we prove superpolynomial decay of finite-grid total variation error in the number of MH updates, with constants that do not grow with guidance depth. The error prefactor tends to zero as the value functions approach exact Doob values and the time grid is refined.

entries.title: Unlearning Model Identity: Ablating LoRA Weights from Question-Based Identity Tuning
entries.abstract: Large Language Models are trained on diverse corpora containing outputs from proprietary teacher models and provider-curated sources. Models subsequently inherit embedded self-identity traits, persistently asserting specific proprietary names. Service providers of open-weight models frequently require the removal of model identity for downstream applications, such as custom interfaces, without exposing provider affiliations to end-users. Effective identity modification is therefore critical for customized model alignment and deployment. This study proposes a method to localize parameter-level representations of self-identity within low-rank adaptation modules to perform targeted weight ablation. By generating probing questions designed to elicit self-naming outputs and fine-tuning the base model on these responses, the approach identifies and ablates high-magnitude weights within the parameter set. Experimental results demonstrate that distilled identity traits reside within a localized subset of low-rank weights, achieving a complete removal rate in Qwen3.5-2B and a 10% rate in Gemma4-E2B while preserving general task capabilities. These findings confirm that ablating top-tier adaptation weights suppresses distilled self-identification without compromising broader model performance.

entries.title: Aegis: A Conversational Prototype for Lung Cancer Risk Information and Follow-up
entries.abstract: Collecting self-reported risk information and maintaining continuity between assessment, explanation, and follow-up are practical components of a lung cancer screening workflow. We present Aegis, a browser-based research prototype that combines a conversational questionnaire, rule-based risk categorization, downloadable reports, retrieval-augmented health information, and doctor-user communication. A session-oriented controller manages question progression and clarification, while a language model assists with answer validation. Structured responses are passed to a separate risk-analysis module, and reports are linked to user and session records through Firebase services. The project adopts a multi-agent design that separates information collection, validation, assessment, and report generation. Its documented verification scope comprises 45 functional test specifications covering account management, questionnaire interaction, reporting, doctor-side review, and consultation. The available evaluation describes workflow behavior qualitatively; it provides no per-case execution results, clinical cohort, predictive-performance measurements, or comparative experiments. We therefore present Aegis as an engineering prototype for organizing risk information and follow-up, with clinical validity and the benefits of its agent-based design remaining unestablished. The paper describes the implementation, distinguishes implemented workflows from incomplete extensions, and identifies the evidence required for reproducible and clinically meaningful evaluation.
entries.comment: 30 pages, including 12 pages of main text and references and 18 pages of supplementary material; 27 references. All authors contributed equally and share first authorship

entries.title: Self-prediction residuals improve single-pass detection of wrong-object boxes in grounded vision-language models
entries.abstract: Grounded vision-language models write boxes as text, and the mean probability of their coordinate tokens says little about whether a box is right. We study a single-pass signal for boxes on another object, which matter when only the object counts. A linear map, fitted per model to its own answers without labels, reads a box from the hidden state before writing. Its disagreement with the written box, the self-prediction residual, flags boxes on another object although the read-out is far less accurate; the residual's weight was fixed with labels on two models. On a replication list of 1,200 RefCOCOg test items, the residual, averaged over six models, raises the detection of these errors for each of fifteen single-pass scores, by 0.026 to 0.049 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) on a label-free probe and probes trained on 2,000 labelled items. Over all errors, adding it to the label-free probe moves AUROC, averaged over the models, by less than 0.02 (95% interval). With a fifth of answers reviewed, the share of all errors caught moves from 0.518 to 0.524, that of boxes on another object from 0.505 to 0.607 (post hoc): the residual changes which errors are found, not how many, and in cost-weighted recall it breaks even when such a box costs about 0.86 times another error, and its gain is positive in point estimate at equal costs. These gains come from RefCOCOg lists of MS-COCO images.
entries.comment: 35 pages, 5 figures; supplementary material included (65 pages). Code: https://github.com/chen4study-hub/spred

entries.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
entries.abstract: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity O(SAH⁴/ε²), where S, A, and H denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of H to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of Ω(SAH⁴/ε²) shows that the resulting H⁴ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size η=1/H requires Ω(H²/ε) iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

entries.title: Neural Schrödinger Bridge via Yasue Action with Applications to Generative Modeling
entries.abstract: We propose a novel neural solver for inferring the continuous state evolution of the Schrödinger bridge problem. The proposed solver builds on a saddle point formulation involving the Yasue action functional. This allows us to realize the continuous state evolution by learning the optimal velocity for an ordinary differential equation, as opposed to learning the optimal drift for a stochastic differential equation. The proposed solver only uses the source and the target samples, and not the source and target distributions per se, which makes it particularly suitable for high dimensional applications arising in generative modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solver using several numerical experiments in low and high dimensions, using both real and synthetic datasets.

entries.title: Interpreting Diffusion Model Activations in Natural Language
entries.abstract: Interpreting the intermediate activations of diffusion models (DMs) is key to understanding how they generate images. Existing interpretability methods for DMs provide limited support for open-ended interrogation, making it difficult to extract human-interpretable insights. We extend LatentQA, the task of answering natural-language questions about Large Language Model activations, to DM activations. We introduce the Diffusion-specific Activation Oracle (DAO), which translates DM activations into natural-language answers to open-ended questions about the ongoing generation. Our experiments show that DAO can effectively describe the content of the final image from activations at early denoising steps. Additionally, we demonstrate that DAO captures the structure of the DM's activation space well enough to steer image generation toward target attributes. Furthermore, we show that attribution patching through DAO identifies DM components that contribute to visual attributes specified in natural language. Our code is available at https://github.com/yamanoko/dao/tree/main.

entries.title: Fast World Planner: Advantage-Aware Action-Chunk Policy for Online Planning
entries.abstract: Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is central to online planning for model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), but its iterative refinement incurs planning latency. Reducing refinement iterations often degrades performance, motivating stronger policy guidance learned from the planner. However, existing methods typically learn from the planner through action-level alignment, which does not directly capture the complete H-step planner proposal. Moreover, planner imitation leaves further target improvement to online refinement. To address these limitations, we propose FaSt World PlANner (SWAN), an advantage-aware MPPI-based MBRL framework that explicitly represents and improves the complete H-step planner proposal to improve policy guidance for efficient online planning. For proposal representation, SWAN combines k-MPPI, a multimodal MPPI extension, with a mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) action-chunk policy to capture multiple modes and correlations across time and action dimensions. For proposal optimization, we introduce Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization (APO), which reuses MPPI evaluations to construct an improved target using advantage estimates and trains the policy toward this target while preserving planner alignment. Experiments across 31 high-dimensional continuous-control tasks from DMControl, HumanoidBench, and MyoSuite show that SWAN substantially improves control performance and sample efficiency while using 50% fewer MPPI refinement iterations than state-of-the-art planning-based MBRL methods. Finally, SWAN demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree Go2, achieving stable velocity-tracking locomotion with high-frequency control. (see our demo at https://swanfastworldplanner.github.io/)

entries.title: Can Ideologues Agree on Quality? From Non-identifiable Latent Factors to Collective Outcomes
entries.abstract: To surface "objective" fact-check notes, X's Community Notes uses Biased Matrix Factorization (BMF) on crowd-sourced ratings to separate note quality from reviewer ideology. We show that for any correctly specified model that decomposes ratings into quality and ideological alignment, this separation requires fixing an ideological anchor: a reference point for what counts as neutral. We give a characterization for the standard implementation: with L₂ regularization, BMF anchors quality at a point proportional to the mean reviewer ideology, recovering objective quality if and only if the mean reviewer is neutral, assuming note quality is uncorrelated with note leaning. This parallels the Condorcet Jury Theorem: collective judgment recovers truth when the pool is unbiased on average. When that assumption fails, BMF's recovered ranking shifts toward maximizing aggregate reviewer satisfaction, which coincides with social welfare only when the pool is representative. This is not specific to BMF; the rating matrix admits a continuous family of gauge-equivalent decompositions, each implying a different quality ranking, so no mechanism based on ratings alone can recover quality without implicitly choosing such an anchor. What appears to be routine hyperparameter tuning is in fact a normative choice about whose preferences define quality.

entries.title: Action-Conditioned Transition Irreversibility for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Reinforcement Learning
entries.abstract: Reinforcement-learning agents shape the observations they encounter; consequently, detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) states requires analysing action-conditioned trajectories rather than treating inputs as independent samples. We propose Action-Conditioned Transition Irreversibility (ACTI), a detector that evaluates forward and backward transition likelihoods, calibrates this comparison against the in-distribution profile at each timestep, and smooths the score over a short window, using no future information. We tested ACTI across six environments and fifteen detectors within OOD-RL-Bench, using the four anomaly mechanisms that qualified in every environment, with ten policy replicates per environment. All primary metrics are matched-time: each score after anomaly onset is compared with a clean twin rollout's score at the same timestep. Our method secured the top macro matched-time AUROC, outperforming the dynamics-model baseline (PEDM), while scoring transitions roughly two orders of magnitude faster. Compared to the state-only variant, ACTI achieved a small but consistent AUROC gain and a shorter detection delay. The capacity-matched forward-only baseline, ACTI-Forward, secured a statistically significant advantage in AUPRC alongside a reduced detection delay. The discrepancy in AUROC did not reach statistical significance. Ablation studies suggest instead that performance improvements stem from action conditioning, calibration at each timestep, and smoothing of the transition-likelihood scores. Based on these results, we recommend using ACTI-Forward.

entries.title: BitShare: Sensitivity-Aware Binning and Bit Sharing for Compacting LLM Weight Storage
entries.abstract: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.

entries.title: Bridging Teacher-Student Capability Gaps with Recurrent Computation
entries.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from large language models to smaller students, yet stronger teachers do not always yield better students. Recent studies report diminishing or even negative returns from teacher scaling. We hypothesize that these limitations arise in part from insufficient student capacity to absorb the teacher's knowledge. We therefore investigate loop and recurrent computation as a way to expand the student's effective capacity by modifying its computation graph while keeping the backbone parameter count fixed. Under teacher-forced KD during pretraining, weight-shared looping improves performance but retains teacher-size saturation, whereas cross-token recurrence avoids the observed reversal with larger teachers. In mathematical post-training under both teacher-forced KD and on-policy distillation (OPD), recurrent students scale better with increasing teacher size than looped and vanilla LLMs do. Crucially, we show that a pretrained LLM can be readily fine-tuned into a looped or recurrent architecture jointly with OPD, without repeating pretraining. Our recurrent Qwen model improves with larger teachers and consistently outperforms looped and vanilla LLMs. This suggests a new post-training paradigm that integrates architectural conversion into distillation, avoiding a separate conversion stage while substantially improving student performance and maintaining near-vanilla inference latency.

entries.title: DRAM: Memory-Efficient Muon via Rank Reallocation in Principal-Random Subspaces
entries.abstract: Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of O(T^(-1/4)) in the stochastic setting and O(T^(-1/2)) in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.

entries.title: Understanding and Mitigating the Fragility of Self-Rewarding Optimization
entries.abstract: Self-rewarding optimization (SRO) promises to improve language models by enabling them to generate their own reward signals. Yet when and how SRO succeeds or fails remains poorly understood. We reveal that SRO is fundamentally fragile: even seemingly benign perturbations to training prompts can corrupt the self-generated preference signal and trigger iterative collapse. We demonstrate this through two prompt-level attacks that serve as controlled stress tests: a Re-Ranking attack that concentrates training on prompts where self-reward diverges from an oracle, and a Preamble attack that learns short prefixes inflating self-reward without any gain in oracle quality. To explain why these attacks succeed, we introduce self-reward fidelity (SRF), a metric quantifying on-policy agreement between self-evaluated and oracle rewards. We show that SRF can serve as a diagnostic signal of self-supervision reliability, and that controlled SRF perturbations induce a phase-transition region: SRO improves when SRF remains sufficiently high, but collapses once SRF drops below a model- and task-dependent threshold. This analysis motivates Projection Decoupling Defense, which suppresses SRO update components along directions to which the reward generator is locally sensitive, improving SRO robustness under adversarial conditions. This work sheds light on the fragility of SRO and charts promising directions toward making it more robust.

entries.title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
entries.abstract: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution μ, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When μ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When μ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured O(dlogT) mistake bound; When μ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in T and in terms of the VC dimension d, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an O(√dT) balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to poly(dDlogT) factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension D. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.

entries.title: Complex band-limited maximum likelihood: estimating the wave behind detected quanta
entries.abstract: Detected photons and electrons land at positions drawn from |ψ|², yet it is ψ, phase included, that a wave equation propagates, and the state that produced the particles is often known only in part. A density estimator can recover |ψ|² directly from the positions, without any wave equation, but it discards the phase, and with it the state. We introduce complex band-limited maximum likelihood (complex BLML), which estimates ψ itself by maximising the likelihood of the detected positions over exactly the intensities the physics allows: squared moduli of complex functions whose spectrum lies in a given set, such as a band, the shape of the aperture, or several modes for a partially coherent source. A single eigenvalue can certify a global maximum. On simulated two-slit far fields we measure what each prior is worth: a band reaches a given accuracy with seven times fewer photons than a kernel density estimate and already gives the fringe contrast and the relative phase, and the shape of the aperture adds the slit geometry. Some quantities need a prior at any number of photons: for slits of one profile the intensity fixes only the contrast 2ρV/(1+ρ²), and on a line two different apertures can produce the same particles. Cutting a pattern to a few fringes, as published records are, removes the slit width. On four public single-particle double-slit records it predicts held-out particles best among the methods we tested, kernel estimators and two-slit optical models included, and it recovers the fringe contrast without a model of the optics. On fluorescent beads it finds the resolution limit of the microscope, 2NA/λ, from the photons alone.
entries.comment: 13 pages, 6 figures; supplementary material as ancillary file. Submitted to Physical Review A

entries.title: When and Where to Transfer: Learning Transferable Historical Contexts for Short-History Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
entries.abstract: Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to identify informative historical contexts from the sources. This paper proposes Hierarchical Context Transfer (HiCT), a framework that adaptively weights source groups and their historical contexts to determine both where and when to transfer. A shared context encoder and cross-attention are used to learn weights over source groups and historical contexts. These weights guide regularized transfer estimation, followed by an optional target-specific correction. This paper establishes a target excess-risk bound for the context-weighted transfer estimator. Experiments demonstrate competitive predictive performance across four multivariate forecasting datasets and a favorable accuracy–runtime trade-off against the evaluated baselines. Source-corruption ablations illustrate the roles of group-level and within-group weighting in adapting to unreliable source histories.

entries.title: SAFE-DRIFT: Data Selection for Supervised Fine-tuning with Controllable Off-Target Drifts
entries.abstract: We propose SAFE-DRIFT, a data-selection framework for supervised fine-tuning that improves a target capability while controlling unwanted drift in the model's other behaviors. We formalize this as a constrained optimization problem that maximizes alignment with the target gradient, subject to a budget on off-target drift which we quantify using the Fisher information of a reference distribution. Under this objective, the optimal, closed-form update is a damped natural-gradient step that downweights reference-sensitive directions. To estimate these high-dimensional gradients and work within the right geometry, we further derive a scalable algorithm that approximates the Fisher information and the target gradient in a shared low-dimensional subspace and analyze how entanglement of the target and reference task can affect the update. We evaluate SAFE-DRIFT against state-of-the-art data selection methods across diverse domains including coding and medical question answering, yielding competitive target performance while reducing degradation on specified off-target behaviors.

entries.title: DisSparse: Pipelined Top-p Sparse Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
entries.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-k selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-k uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-p (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-p sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-p kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-p methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

entries.title: State of Mind: Learning and Evaluating World Models of Naturalistic Brain Dynamics
entries.abstract: Understanding naturalistic brain activity requires going beyond the stimulus alone, as external inputs continuously interact with an individual's evolving brain state. A world model captures such dynamics in a latent state by inferring it from neural observations, predicting stimulus-driven evolution, and updating with new observations. However, existing brain world models fail to maintain a persistent latent state over time, and standard metrics of neural prediction accuracy cannot tell whether a model tracks an individual's brain state or relies solely on the stimulus. To directly test state inference, prediction, and updating, we introduce BrainStateBench, which evaluates a model's latent state through a frozen linear probe on whole-cortex, movie-driven fMRI. Its State task tests whether a model captures trial-to-trial variability in an individual's responses to repeated stimuli, while Forecast and Updating evaluate future activity predictions without and with new observations, respectively. To track individual brain state across time, we propose Spectator, a linear latent world model trained with a joint-embedding predictive objective. Spectator encodes short- and long-horizon observation histories into a two-timescale latent state and predicts state transitions linearly from the current state and stimulus. Stimulus-only encoders reach 0.320 in fMRI prediction correlation without observing the brain (0% on State), while prior deep brain world models reach 0.239 yet score at most 0.4% on State. In contrast, Spectator achieves 0.349 correlation alongside 5.5% on State, 16.0% on Forecast, and 20.3% on Updating, outperforming all baselines while forecasting over 20x faster than deep forecasting models.

entries.title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation
entries.abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x–13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8–67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed (α∈[1.88, 2.20]). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1–v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
entries.comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Open weights (Apache-2.0), shard provenance manifests, and Rust Jacobi SVD spectral certificates: https://huggingface.co/VaidhyaMegha/Shoonya

entries.title: An equivariant classical density functional for ionic fluids at complex interfaces
entries.abstract: Predicting the combined effects of ionic packing and long-range electrostatics at complex interfaces is technologically important, but remains challenging without atomistic simulations. Here we present a machine-learned classical density functional for ionic fluids that combines a symmetry-adapted neural free energy for short-range correlations with explicit long-range electrostatics. Trained on three-dimensional equilibrium densities and bulk correlations of the full-Coulomb restricted primitive model, a single functional transfers to charge-patterned particles and atomically structured electrodes. Around anisotropic charged solutes, it reproduces the ionic structure and mean forces from molecular dynamics, including reversals of the bare electrostatic force. At metal electrodes, self-consistent coupling to metal atoms captures the redistribution of ionic and electrode charge and the loading-dependent capacitance enhancement produced by steps and bumps. Combined with mobilities determined independently from bulk molecular dynamics, the same functional describes the main features of charging dynamics and resolves geometry-dependent spatial relaxation. This framework can be extended to more complex ionic fluids, enabling efficient exploration of how composition and geometry control structure and response.

entries.title: Accelerating wave-scattering simulations with learned search directions
entries.abstract: Wave-scattering simulation requires solving a dense boundary-element system for every frequency, incidence and design. Krylov solvers build each search space from scratch, and it grows with problem size. Here we present BEMFormer, a solver that learns to generate search directions across systems of one integral equation and supplies geometry-specific directions through a coarse-grid correction. BEMFormer generalizes to unseen geometries, meshes and excitations, and to acoustic scattering after fine-tuning on eight geometries. It reproduces the measured radar cross-sections of benchmark targets. On a quadcopter with 1.04 million unknowns, 38 times the largest training problem, BEMFormer solves each system 30 times faster than a preconditioned Krylov solver. Both reach a radar cross-section deviation of about 1 dB, comparable to the difference between independent measurements and acceptable for engineering applications. These results show that solving million-unknown scattering problems in minutes is possible when the search space is learned rather than built from scratch.

entries.title: SoK: Splitting the Trigger or Adding Attackers? Disentangling Distributed Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning
entries.abstract: Distributed backdoor attacks split a trigger among several federated learning clients, so that the backdoor appears only in the aggregated model. Since DBA, a line of work has reported that such attacks are stronger, more persistent, and stealthier than a single attacker with the full trigger. We systematize this literature and test this belief. We code nineteen primary studies and fifteen papers that evaluate against DBA. The reported advantage is rarely measured against a complete trigger delivered by the same attackers, and none of the fifteen evaluations tests whether individual pieces remain effective. We then run 875 paired federated runs that separate adding attackers from splitting the trigger. In our image experiments, adding attackers raised attack success in every seed of all 30 cells where we measured it, by 7.5 to 83.4 percentage points on average. Splitting the trigger among the same attackers had a smaller effect, and its sign depended on the piece layout, the allocation, and the attackers' local training. With DBA's compact layout, splitting lowered attack success on CIFAR-10. A larger penalty on small CNNs vanished once the attackers trained longer, and an FCBA-style allocation gained a few points. Widely separated pieces helped on CIFAR-10, its grayscale version, and GTSRB. No model required all pieces. Neural Cleanse suppressed single pieces together with the full trigger, but split backdoors with separated pieces survived it better than complete ones. We derive reporting requirements for attack and defense evaluations.
entries.comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 22 tables. Systematization of knowledge with original controlled experiments (875 paired federated learning runs). Under submission. Code and data: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/fl-pieces-artifact-BFF3/

entries.title: AMP-OD: Active Model Probing for Unsupervised Outlier Model Selection–Extended Version
entries.abstract: Outlier detection is often deployed in fully unsupervised settings, where labels are unavailable and practitioners must choose a detector without direct performance feedback. Existing unsupervised outlier model selection methods predict detector quality from static meta-features and historical performance on meta-datasets, but they commit before observing how any detector behaves on the target dataset. We propose AMP-OD, an execution-conditioned probe-then-commit framework. AMP-OD runs a small number of inexpensive probe detectors, uses their score patterns as target-dataset evidence, and then selects a final detector from a larger candidate pool. To interpret unlabeled probe responses, we introduce a Leave-One-Out Family Probe Posterior (LOO-FPP), which converts probe score patterns into gated detector-family evidence while reducing self-validation in pseudo-label construction. AMP-OD further combines this evidence with historical reliability through a warm-start prior, a sequential probe/stop policy, and lower-confidence-bound arbitration. Extensive experiments and ablation studies show that detector responses provide useful evidence beyond static meta-features, with the LOO-FPP and conservative arbitration as key contributors.
entries.comment: 25 pages. An extended version of "AMP-OD: Active Model Probing for Unsupervised Outlier Model Selection" accepted at KDD 2027

entries.title: Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights
entries.abstract: We show that an AI agent can write new capabilities into a pretrained language model by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons inside its existing layers, without backpropagation and without fitting any weight to the answers of task examples. It has a budget of 50 model passes and sees no validation or test instance. Composed in one model, its modules for six BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) subtasks raise the normalized BBH score of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 19.95 to 41.05 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: at most 35.01) and that of Gemma-3-1B-it from 10.25 to 32.86. Against the unmodified model at the same precision, both composites leave the next-token distribution on 1,023,000 WikiText tokens unchanged (KL exactly 0), give identical answers on 15,845 items of five other Leaderboard tests and identical scores on the other 18 BBH subtasks. The agent also writes exact multiplication up to 20 digits, running the model only up to 6 (100.0% on the absent lengths of the sealed test in both models; a LoRA with the same budget: at most 2.1%). Sets, rules and report sentences were sealed in git before the first session (manifests timestamped in Bitcoin), with dated amendments listed in Appendix D; a frozen evaluator ran the sealed test once. Verdicts (H5: tracking; H6: composite; H8: one pass vs. chain of thought; H9: fresh and rewritten instances; H10: side effects; H12: multiplication), on the preregistered sealed test, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H9 success, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success; Gemma-3-1B-it (H7: H5, H6, H8 and H9 in this model): H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H8 (tracking 3) success, H9 partial, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success. Not everything worked: 4 of 45 single modules show small side effects and 5 of 50 sessions hit the 12-hour limit without a module.

entries.title: Digital Knockoffs
entries.abstract: Social simulations often use language model agents to represent people who differ on several measurable traits. However, describing a trait profile in a prompt does not guarantee the agent will express each trait at its intended level. We propose a method that calibrates agents to multidimensional profiles using activation steering: (i) extract steering directions for each trait, (ii) learn a shared mapping from steering strengths to measured trait scores, and (iii) search for a steering intervention for each target. We use Bayesian optimization for this search and evaluate the method on the Big Five personality scores of 500 OpenPsychometrics respondents. In each of five rounds, the assigned interventions yield lower mean absolute error across respondents than the prompting and steering baselines. Further, the model's responses to a given intervention yield the same trait profile regardless of whose target motivated it, so a poor match for one respondent can be the best match for another. When we match each respondent to the closest profile found across all tested interventions, Bayesian optimization yields 16.6% lower mean absolute error than uniform random search at the same evaluation budget. Our method thus offers a way to build social agents whose measured traits dovetail with those of the people they seek to represent. Whether this closer fit translates to improved predictions of downstream behavior remains an open question.

entries.title: ESM-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Whether AI Agents Understand Earth System Model Physics and Code
entries.abstract: AI coding agents that modify Earth System Model (ESM) code must preserve both software interfaces and the physical assumptions encoded in them. We introduce ESM-Bench, a benchmark of 60 developer-commit tasks from 6 repositories: Noah-MP, CLM5, SUMMA, ParFlow, MOM6, and VIC. The v5 corpus contains 17 physics-based bug fixes, 16 process-representation modifications, 13 parameterization-scheme selections, and 14 parameter-optimization tasks. Each task includes a scientific objective, parent-commit source files, a reference diff, and three stored prompt variants. An artifact audit confirms that all 60 reference diffs apply to their supplied starting files. We define an eight-item patch-review rubric and audit five archived patch fixtures against the implemented local checkers. None of the five fixture diffs applies to its supplied starting files, yet three text-pattern checkers return a pass. A ParFlow expression replay disagrees with the reference slopes, and a MOM6 pattern check detects an omitted update. Inspection also identifies a retained VIC reference assignment that overwrites the intended vegetation-specific albedo. These findings expose limits of reference patches and local proxies as correctness evidence. The release provides a reproducible corpus and diagnostic tools; complete expert validation, comparative agent performance, and full-model execution remain unmeasured on v5.

entries.title: PAMS: Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-tuning
entries.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization provides a computationally efficient approach to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), but conventional methods typically rely on isotropic perturbations that ignore the anisotropic structure of neural-network parameter spaces. We introduce Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace (PAMS), a ZO optimization framework that uses forward-pass activation statistics to construct structured, layer-wise perturbation geometries without computing gradients or forming dense curvature matrices. PAMS tracks a low-rank approximation of the dominant activation subspace and its associated spectrum online, and uses the spectrum to softly reweight perturbation variance while preserving exploration in directions outside the retained subspace. A trace normalization separates the perturbation geometry from its overall scale, enabling consistent perturbation magnitudes across layers. We show theoretically that the resulting perturbation covariance induces right-side preconditioning of the gradient of the corresponding Gaussian-smoothed objective. We further characterize the estimator's smoothing bias and second moment and derive a nonconvex convergence guarantee that captures the effects of the perturbation geometry and smoothing radius. The proposed low-rank tracking procedure requires O(n_l r) persistent memory for a layer with input dimension nl and retained rank r, avoiding the O(n_l²) memory required by a dense activation covariance. Experiments on transformer-based language-model fine-tuning tasks across GLUE and SuperGLUE demonstrate that PAMS improves the effectiveness and stability of zeroth-order optimization while retaining its gradient-free and objective-evaluation-based advantages.

entries.title: A hybrid Graph-based Machine Learning Model for predicting Delivery Times in Supply Chain Logistics
entries.abstract: Global supply chains are increasingly vulnerable to disruptions arising from external events, such as natural disasters and geopolitical crises, and from internal operational inefficiencies, including supplier delays and bottlenecks in order shipping. This work, conducted within the Horizon Europe project M4ESTRO, introduces a hybrid modelling approach combining graph theory and machine learning to represent supply chain logistics operations, with a focus on predicting delays in inbound flows between industrial suppliers and manufacturing entities. The various stages of order fulfilment are modelled through a formal mathematical framework, by defining disruption indicators computed from both historical and real-time data drawn from heterogeneous sources, including traffic and weather conditions and supplier dispatch readiness. Building on a graph-based representation of the supply chain, stochastic methods based on Markov chains are applied to estimate delivery times, detect schedule deviations, quantify prediction uncertainty, and produce interpretable metrics to support operational decision-making. Within the M4ESTRO project, the proposed framework was applied to build a web application for real-time tracking of inbound logistics, and was validated in a use case with an industrial project partner. The web application successfully enabled early detection of logistics disruptions along the supply chain and provided stakeholders with the visibility needed to act before delays propagated. The underlying model proved effective as the basis of a resilient, data-driven logistics tracking system, aligned with the digital transformation objectives of industry and with Manufacturing-as-a-Service paradigms.
entries.comment: 45 pages, 14 figures, 24 tables. To be published in Open Research Europe

entries.title: HiPPO Functional Memory: Coordinate-Queryable Attention for Irregular Time Series
entries.abstract: Irregular time series are recorded at nonuniform times and are often queried at other times: between observations, after the last one, or on a regular grid. Continuous-time models answer such queries by integrating latent dynamics, and time-aware attention models answer them by revisiting the observation tokens. We introduce HiPPO Functional Memory (HiPPO-FM), an attention operator that writes an irregular history into a rank-M function space with explicit time coordinates. Masked self-attention first exchanges content among the observations; the updated values are then contracted against kernel-smoothed HiPPO-Legendre features and solved through a regularized Gram matrix, so the retained coefficients define a function that is read at any time through the same features. The write and read have the form of an interdomain sparse Gaussian-process mean: every readout lies in an M-dimensional reproducing-kernel subspace, and a pointwise bound separates the approximation error of this subspace from the error of the learned memory. Removing the functional memory from the encoder raises Spiral reconstruction RMSE 18-fold. The full model has the lowest error in 11 of 12 Spiral settings, the highest overall accuracy and best average rank on 20 irregular UEA datasets, the highest event-type accuracy on all five multi-type event benchmarks, and a 21% lower extrapolation MSE than CRU on PhysioNet. Because the memory has fixed rank, the state retained after encoding keeps a fixed size as the history grows and is 102 times smaller than a token cache at 1,024 observations.

entries.title: Optimal User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization and Mean Estimation with Heavy Tails
entries.abstract: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under (ε, δ)-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and k-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only O(1/ε) users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional d/ε user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

entries.title: When a Permitted Action Completes a Forbidden Workflow: Designing Consequence-Oriented Approval for LLM Agents
entries.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents increasingly ask people to approve consequential actions, yet an approval prompt shows only the next step. A request to send a file to an approved recipient can look harmless even when that file was assembled, several steps earlier, from data the user said must never leave. We call this a cumulative authorization failure and argue that it is an interaction design problem as much as a security problem. The evidence a reviewer needs is spread across the trajectory, and listing it in time order leaves the reviewer to reconstruct the causal chain. We present the Cumulative Consent Ledger (CCL), an approval interface built on four design principles that restate the user's intent, bind the review to the exact action, compose the cumulative consequence, and keep every claim checkable. A trusted monitor that tracks artifact lineage supplies the evidence. In a between-subjects study with 80 participants and 960 approval decisions, CCL was associated with fewer unsafe approvals than an evidence-matched chronological log (24.2% vs. 32.5%), higher comprehension, and faster decisions, although the adjusted difference in unsafe approvals remained uncertain (-7.9 points, 95% CrI [-19.7, 3.8]). In a system evaluation, the monitor detected 89.2% of 120 violating checkpoints and, used as an execution gate, reduced executed unsafe effects from 43.3% to 5.0% for one agent at a small cost to benign completion. We derive implications for designing consent around consequences rather than individual calls.
entries.comment: Under Review at the 41st AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-27)

entries.title: Guidance-Induced Activation of Score Estimation Errors in Diffusion Models
entries.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional score estimates to steer diffusion sampling. The weighted-solenoidal component of each score error has no instantaneous effect on the evolution of its corresponding reference density. Because the guided density in CFG generally differs from both reference densities, the combination of these solenoidal components can affect the evolution of the guided marginals. We call this mechanism guidance-induced error activation. Using a weighted Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition, we identify the activated error field, quantify its magnitude, and characterize when it vanishes. At fixed noise time, the activated error field varies continuously with guidance strength. Its weak first-order variation has two terms, one from reweighting the errors and one from the change in the guided density. For finite score errors, ODE characteristics and an SDE Feynman-Kac formula connect error-activation to the generated densities. For a class of finite Gaussian mixtures, error-activation can account for most of the KL divergence between the generated distributions by learned-score and exact-score CFG ODE samplers under strong guidance. Ideal score filtering removes the weighted-solenoidal errors and eliminates error-activation. Controlled experiments with Gaussian and Gamma mixtures illustrate how activation affects the generated densities. Qualitative CIFAR-10 comparisons suggest that filtering can help preserve object structure under strong guidance.

entries.title: PFN-Syn: Generating Synthetic Tabular Data with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
entries.abstract: Synthetic tabular data can help enable data sharing and model development in privacy-sensitive domains, but existing generators often require dataset-specific training and substantial computation. We introduce PFN-Syn, a training-free framework for synthetic tabular data generation based on prior-data fitted networks. We evaluate PFN-Syn against training-based generators on eight binary classification datasets. PFN-Syn achieves the highest average downstream utility among evaluated synthetic generators, with higher generation throughput than training-based baselines, while maintaining competitive distributional similarity and distance-to-closest-record privacy behavior. Our results suggest that tabular foundation models can serve as useful building blocks for practical synthetic tabular data generation.
entries.comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. VLDB 2026 Workshop: Tabular Data Analysis (TaDA). Code: https://github.com/brains-group/table-agent-toolkit

entries.title: Lean Census: A Distributional Analysis of AI-Generated Lean Code
entries.abstract: We compare two human-written and four AI-generated Lean libraries with Mathlib through the distributions of simple statistics of their code. For each library we measure inline claims in proofs, proof length, how often each declaration is used, and design choices such as instances and private declarations, and we read each against the variation among Mathlib's own areas. The AI-generated libraries have more inline claims per theorem, longer proofs, fewer instances, and more private declarations than the human-written ones. We release the code for the analysis as a package, lean-census, at https://github.com/project-numina/lean-census.

entries.title: Targeted Learning for Externally Controlled Trials and Beyond
entries.abstract: This paper focuses on externally controlled trials (ECTs), which consist of a single-arm clinical trial supplemented by an external control arm (ECA). Potential data sources for the ECA can be broadly classified into three categories: (i) the control arm of a historical clinical trial, (ii) a concurrent cohort study, and (iii) external real-world data (RWD). In this paper, we consider a broad class of estimands defined through balancing weights. For a given estimand in the class, we discuss the efficient influence function (EIF) and the targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE), together with practical implementation algorithms. Within the targeted learning framework, TMLE is a substitution estimator that enjoys several desirable theoretical properties and favorable finite-sample performance. Finally, the proposed framework is extended to two additional settings: (1) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) augmented with external covariate information to define a target population, and (2) indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) that combine individual patient data (IPD) from an internal RCT with aggregate data (AgD) from an external RCT.

entries.title: Center-Aware Ordinal Learning for Prostate Cancer Grading from Histopathology Images
entries.abstract: Prostate cancer grading from histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) is complicated by the ordered nature of ISUP grades, class imbalance, and center-dependent variations in staining, tissue preparation, and scanning. Most weakly supervised methods treat grade groups as independent categories and may therefore learn representations that do not transfer reliably across institutions. We propose a center-aware ordinal learning framework that combines a pretrained pathology encoder with attention-based multiple instance learning. The framework uses an Earth Mover's Distance loss to account for ordinal errors, an ordinal supervised contrastive objective to align same-grade slides across centers while separating grades according to disease severity, and curriculum learning to reduce the dominance of benign cases. We evaluate the framework on approximately 9,100 biopsy WSIs from the two-center PANDA dataset. The proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 0.842 and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.958 on the held-out test set. Its main benefit is observed in cross-center transfer: when a linear probe is trained on Karolinska representations and evaluated on Radboud, accuracy increases from 0.643 to 0.823 and quadratic weighted kappa from 0.899 to 0.930. Performance remains stable in the reverse direction. UMAP projections further show improved mixing between centers while preserving an ordinal grade trajectory. These results suggest that combining ordinal and center-aware objectives produces more transferable slide representations for multi-center prostate cancer grading.
entries.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Accepted as an oral presentation at SPIE Medical Imaging 2027

entries.title: WingBench: Benchmarking How AI Agents Search for Better Designs
entries.abstract: Design search often uses cheap learned predictions to choose which candidates deserve expensive tests, but these tests can fail, especially on the unusual designs that optimization favors. We introduce WingBench, a multifidelity benchmark in which optimizers and AI agents design transonic wings with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) inside the search. They can query a learned aerodynamic surrogate and spend a fixed budget of sequential CFD evaluations, each returning a score or a failure type. WingBench grades the design each method recommends, reporting separately whether it receives a valid score and how good that score is. Using WingBench, we contribute a study of five baseline optimizers and a comparison of three AI agent methods, which produced 6,629 CFD evaluation records.
